newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian leader says ousted prince faces charges.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian leader says ousted prince faces charges.

text.p: Cambodian leader Hun Sen said in a letter to the U.N. secretary-general that Prince Norodom Ranariddh, the co-premier he ousted in early July, was free to return to Cambodia but would have to face charges in court.
Hun Sen also asked Kofi Annan to help in coordinating international observers for Cambodia's next election in May.

"Prince Norodom Ranariddh can still return to Cambodia but he must clear himself in court of the accusations of illegally importing weapons and illegal negotiations with the outlawed Khmer Rouge (guerrilla group)," Hun Sen said in the letter, which was read over government radio on Friday.

Hun Sen ousted Ranariddh on July 6 after two days of fighting in the Cambodian capital. The prince was not in the country at the time and has since dismissed the accusations against him and called for opposition to Hun Sen.
After overthrowing the prince Hun Sen said he wanted to maintain the coalition government with the prince's royalist party and hold elections as scheduled in May.

Hun Sen has said he does not want a large-scale electoral mission similar to that which oversaw a 1993 poll that Ranariddh won, but he said he would accept some international observers coordinated by the United Nations.
"I would like to thank Your Excellency ... to complete the duty of coordinating international observers in the period of the election," Hun Sen said in the letter.
Cambodian Foreign Minister Ung Huot was formally appointed first prime minister on Thursday, replacing Ranariddh after King Norodom Sihanouk, the prince's father, dropped his opposition to the move.
The United States on Thursday said it would deal with Ung Huot, who will maintain his post as foreign minister, even though it considered the process of his selection undemocratic.

More than two-thirds of Cambodia's National Assembly members voted on Wednesday by secret ballot to accept Ung Huot's nomination but an official at the U.S. embassy in Phnom Penh said given the climate of intimidation following Hun Sen's coup, the vote could not be considered democratic.

"We'll be meeting with him in order to do business with the government of Cambodia ... But we do not believe that he was chosen democratically," U.S. State Department spokesman James Rubin told a news briefing in Washington.

After the coup, the United States suspended aid to Cambodia for 30 days while it assessed the situation and Hun Sen's pledge to comply with the 1991 Paris accords that ended Cambodia's civil war. That period expires this weekend.
"I wouldn't expect any significant changes in how we've approached it (aid), and that is that we will not provide funds to go through the government of Cambodia," Rubin said.

Khmer Rouge guerrilla radio, which went off the air without explanation on Thursday, said in a Friday broadcast that everything Hun Sen had done since the coup, in terms of political and military organisation, must be cancelled.
The radio condemned Hun Sen and said guerrillas still regarded Ranariddh as Cambodia's legal first prime minister.

The guerrillas purged their notorious leader Pol Pot late last month after he opposed an alliance with Ranariddh and his royalist party. More than one million people died during the 1975-79 Khmer Rouge rule.
